title: Every Letter in a Military Aircraft Name Explained

lines.text: The F-35 should have been called the F-24.
Under the rules, the next new American fighter after the YF-23 should have taken the next number in line: twenty-four.
Instead, the winning demonstrator, the X-35, simply kept its number. And that's a clue. Every letter and number in a military aircraft name is supposed to follow a system.
Before nineteen sixty-two, the Navy and the Air Force each had their own. The same fighter was the F four H Phantom to the Navy, and the F one ten to the Air Force.
The old Navy name packed in the maker, too. F for fighter, four for the fourth fighter from that company, and H for McDonnell.
Defense Secretary Robert McNamara reportedly found that maddening. So in nineteen sixty-two, the Pentagon replaced them with one system, and the Phantom became simply the F-4.
The full name has six parts: status, modified mission, basic mission, vehicle type, design number, and series letter. Only the basic mission, the number, and the series letter are always required.
Start with the one letter every aircraft must have: the basic mission.
A is attack, built for hitting targets on land or at sea. B is bomber. C is cargo. F is fighter.
Then the rarer ones. E for special electronics. P for maritime patrol. S for anti-submarine warfare. T for trainer. U for utility. And X for special research.
Two letters on the list are strange. K for tanker and R for reconnaissance exist as basic missions, but no ordinary aircraft has ever been given one the way the rules intended.
Utility was once used as a cover. The U-2 spy plane was labeled utility to hide what it really did.
And the line between attack and fighter has blurred. Today, an F can also be a multirole jet that strikes ground targets.
The Air Force even gave the F to the F-117 Nighthawk, a stealth jet built for ground attack, with no official air-to-air role.
For years, people were convinced a secret F-19 stealth fighter existed. In July nineteen eighty-six, the Air Force sealed off a crash site in California, and the rumors exploded.
The jet that crashed was actually an F-117, still classified at the time. No real F-19 has ever been shown to exist.
Meanwhile, the A-10 is the only aircraft in today's Air Force that still carries a plain A.
Next comes the modified mission: an extra letter in front, for an aircraft rebuilt, or built, for a different job.
The best example is the C-130 Hercules, a cargo plane.
Put an A in front, and the AC-130 is a gunship. H makes it a rescue aircraft. M makes it special operations. E makes it electronic warfare. And K makes it a tanker.
Same airframe. One letter changes the job.
That's why the Air Force's newest tanker is the KC-46. K for tanker, on top of C for cargo.
The rest of the list works the same way. W is weather reconnaissance, which is why the Air Force's hurricane hunters are W C one thirties.
V is VIP transport. The President's Boeing seven forty-seven is the V C twenty-five, and the President's newest helicopter is the V H ninety-two.
L means modified for cold weather. The L C one thirty has skis, for landing on ice.
And M and U look alike, but they're split by the kind of mission. M aircraft fly combat and special operations. U aircraft fly support, like the U H sixty Black Hawk.
The vehicle type sits right before the dash, and most airplanes don't need one at all.
H means helicopter, like the AH-64 Apache: an attack helicopter.
V means vertical or short takeoff, like the MV-22 Osprey.
And Q means unmanned. So the MQ-9 Reaper reads as multi-mission, unmanned, design number nine.
There's even a letter for a spaceplane, and one for the ground stations that fly drones.
In front of everything sits the status prefix, for aircraft that aren't in normal service.
X means experimental. Y means prototype. That's why the jet that flew in the competition was the YF-22, and the one that entered service was the F-22.
J and N mean special test, temporary or permanent. And G means permanently grounded.
After the dash comes the design number. In nineteen sixty-two, the counts were restarted, which is why the numbers suddenly got small again.
Then the series letter marks each version: A, then B, then C. The letters I and O are skipped, so they're never confused with one and zero.
There was never an F-4H Phantom, either. That letter was skipped to avoid confusion with its old Navy name, F four H.
And the number thirteen has been skipped in many series, for superstition.
Then there are the rule breakers.
The SR-71 Blackbird continued the old bomber numbers. It was set to be called RS-71, but Air Force chief Curtis LeMay preferred SR, for strategic reconnaissance. And SR is what stuck.
The B-21 skipped ahead, because it's the first bomber of the twenty-first century. The next number in line was three.
The MV-75, the Army's new tiltrotor, jumped all the way to seventy-five, to honor the year the Army was founded, seventeen seventy-five.
The T-6 Texan Two skipped four and five, as a tribute to the original T-6 trainer.
The F-47 was chosen partly to honor the P-47 Thunderbolt, and nineteen forty-seven, the year the Air Force was founded.
Some numbers simply copy the maker. A tanker sold abroad became the K C seven sixty-seven, straight from Boeing's model number.
And the F/A-18 Hornet has a slash that the system doesn't even allow. By the rules, it should have been the AF-18.
So, the next time you see a name like MQ-9A, read it left to right. Multi-mission. Unmanned. Design nine. First version.
And if the number looks wrong, like F-35, there's usually a story behind it.
Which aircraft name should I decode next? Tell me in the comments.
